title: System Design Interview - An insiders guide volume 3
labels: 1:But if we do a math operation

blocks.text: This method of assigning tasks works well when the number of servers is fixed, and the data is spread evenly across them. However, issues occur when new servers are added or existing servers are taken away.

For instance, if server 1 goes offline, then there are only 3 servers left. If we use the same way to sort data or requests (using a hash function), we will still get the same result—this is the hash value for a key. But if we do a math operation to find the server (called modular operation), it gives us different server numbers since we now have one less server.

Server Index | Key | New Server Index
1 | A | 0
2 | B | 1
3 | C | 2
4 | D | Invalid
5 | E | Invalid
Using hash % 3 (the number of remaining servers), we see how the keys are redistributed among the servers. Figure 5-2 displays this new setup of keys according to Table 5-2.

script:
Removing a server impacts how data is distributed. When server 1 goes offline, we have only three servers left. If we keep using the same hash function, we still calculate hash values for keys. But for distribution, we switch to a new modular operation since there’s one less server.

For example, consider the key distribution: key A, previously assigned to server 1, would now shift to server 0. Key B moves to server 1. Key C stays on server 2. Keys D and E end up invalid since there aren’t enough servers.

Table 5-2 shows this clearly. It lists the server index, keys, and their new assignments. Keys shift positions based on the reduced number of servers, illustrating how removing a server changes where data is stored.
